title: Primary Function of the Clevis Linkage
learningObjectives: Connect a real mechanical linkage to its structural load-transfer role.
student: What is the primary structural function of the clevis-pin linkage shown in the industry-context image?
instructor: The clevis-pin linkage transfers tensile load between two rod or linkage members through the yoke, pin, and inner member. The joint provides force transfer while allowing the connection to behave like a pinned mechanical linkage.
gradingNotes: Look for load-transfer language: transfer load, carry tension, transmit force, and maintain a mechanical linkage.
commonMistakes: Students may describe the whole machine without identifying the local connection as the load-transfer element.

title: External Tensile Load
learningObjectives: Identify applied loads and their directions from an idealized diagram.
student: Where are the external loads applied in the simplified problem, and what is their direction?
instructor: Equal and opposite tensile loads {{P}} {{P_unit}} are applied at the far ends of the left and right rods. The left load acts outward to the left, and the right load acts outward to the right, placing the connection in axial tension.
gradingNotes: The industry image does not show force arrows; students should use the problem statement and idealized model.

title: Boundary and Connection Idealization
learningObjectives: Distinguish an axial connector model from a fixed-support beam model.
student: For the idealized connection, identify the effective boundary/loading conditions used in the mechanics model.
instructor: This is not a fixed-support beam or frame problem. The surrounding machine members impose an axial tensile load {{P}} {{P_unit}} at each rod end. The clevis and inner member are connected by the pin at A, which transfers load while allowing the joint to be idealized as a pinned connector.
commonMistakes: A common error is inventing wall reactions or treating the clevis body as a support bracket instead of a tensile load-transfer connection.

title: Load Path Through the Connection
learningObjectives: Trace force transfer through a multi-part mechanical connection.
student: Using the component list, trace the load path through the connection from the left rod to the right rod.
instructor: One acceptable load path is left rod → yoke/clevis → pin at A → inner member → right rod. The same path may be stated in reverse. The pin must be included because it transfers load between the forked yoke and the inner member.
gradingNotes: Missing the pin usually indicates the student has not understood the connection mechanism.

title: Critical Components for the Simplified Check
learningObjectives: Identify which components are checked by the simplified mechanics model.
student: Which components or locations are likely to be critical for this simplified analysis?
instructor: The left rod and right rod are critical for average axial normal stress. The pin at A is critical for average shear stress. In a detailed design, the yoke arms and inner member holes may also be critical because of bearing, tear-out, net-section tension, stress concentration, pin bending, and fatigue.

title: Mechanical Response by Component
learningObjectives: Match each component to the stress quantity used in the base analysis.
student: For each critical component, identify the relevant mechanical response or failure mechanism considered in this problem.
instructor: Left rod: average axial normal stress, σ1 = P/A1. Right rod: average axial normal stress, σ2 = P/A2. Pin A: average shear stress, τA = P/(nsAA), with ns = {{n_s}} for double shear. Bearing stress, pin bending, fatigue, and stress concentration are not included in the simplified calculation.
gradingNotes: The double-shear interpretation is the key conceptual point.

title: Relevant Geometric Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect diameter data to cross-sectional area and average stress.
student: Identify the geometric parameters that control the average normal stress in the rods and the average shear stress in the pin.
instructor: The controlling parameters are d1 = {{d_1}} {{d_1_unit}} for A1 = πd12/4, d2 = {{d_2}} {{d_2_unit}} for A2 = πd22/4, and dA = {{d_A}} {{d_A_unit}} for AA = πdA2/4. Because the pin is in double shear, the total resisting shear area is {{n_s}}AA.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate a physical clevis assembly into a mechanics model.
student: Convert the real clevis-pin linkage into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Your sketch should show the left rod, yoke/clevis, inner member, pin at A, right rod, external tensile load P, rod diameters d1 and d2, and pin diameter dA.
instructor: A correct idealization shows two axial rod members connected through a clevis and pin. The external loads P act outward at both rod ends. The left and right rods carry axial tension. The pin at A is represented as a connector in double shear with two shear planes.
gradingNotes: In a student handout, this can be used as an instructor reference or hidden until after students produce their own sketch.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions that make the average-stress model valid for a first analysis.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real mechanical connection into the simplified Solid Mechanics model.
instructor: Reasonable assumptions include static axial loading; circular prismatic rods at the checked sections; concentric load through each rod; average stress is used; the pin is in double shear; the two shear planes share the load equally; friction, bearing stress, stress concentrations, pin bending, thread effects, clearances, wear, and fatigue are neglected.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the stress calculation before substituting values.
student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence needed to determine the rod normal stresses and pin shear stress.
instructor: Identify the applied tensile load P; compute cross-sectional areas A1 and A2 of the rods; compute pin cross-sectional area AA; recognize that the pin has {{n_s}} shear planes; calculate σ1 = P/A1, σ2 = P/A2, and τA = P/({{n_s}}AA); compare the stress magnitudes and identify the largest calculated average stress.

title: Loading Conditions from the Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Use the instructor diagram to define the base mechanics model.
student: From the instructor diagram, identify the loading conditions and the main connection idealization.
instructor: The connection is subjected to equal and opposite axial tensile loads P = {{P}} {{P_unit}} at the two rod ends. The left rod, yoke, pin, inner member, and right rod form a tensile load path. The pin at A is idealized as a connector in double shear.

title: Internal Loads in Rods and Pin Planes
learningObjectives: Determine internal force in tensile members and load per pin shear plane.
student: Identify the internal load carried by each rod and the shear force carried by each pin shear plane.
instructor: Each rod carries axial force P = {{P}} {{P_unit}} = {{clevis_load_N}} N in tension. The pin transmits the same total load between the yoke and the inner member. Since the pin has {{n_s}} shear planes, each shear plane carries V = P/{{n_s}} = {{clevis_shear_plane_load_N}} N.
commonMistakes: Using the full load on each shear plane doubles the correct average pin shear stress.

title: Cross-Sectional Areas
learningObjectives: Calculate circular cross-sectional areas for rods and pin.
student: Calculate the cross-sectional area of the left rod, right rod, and pin using the given diameters.
instructor: A1 = π({{d_1}} mm)2/4 = {{clevis_area_1_mm2}} mm2. A2 = π({{d_2}} mm)2/4 = {{clevis_area_2_mm2}} mm2. AA = π({{d_A}} mm)2/4 = {{clevis_pin_area_mm2}} mm2. For double shear, the total resisting shear area is {{n_s}}AA = {{clevis_pin_total_shear_area_mm2}} mm2.
gradingNotes: Use N and mm units so stress comes out in N/mm2 = MPa.

title: Average Normal Stress in the Left Rod
learningObjectives: Compute average tensile normal stress from axial force and area.
student: Determine the average normal stress in the left rod.
instructor: σ1 = P/A1 = {{clevis_load_N}} N / {{clevis_area_1_mm2}} mm2 = {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa. The stress is tensile.

title: Average Normal Stress in the Right Rod
learningObjectives: Compute average tensile normal stress for a second member and compare the effect of diameter.
student: Determine the average normal stress in the right rod.
instructor: σ2 = P/A2 = {{clevis_load_N}} N / {{clevis_area_2_mm2}} mm2 = {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa. The stress is tensile. Since the right rod diameter is smaller, it has the larger average normal stress.

title: Pin Shear Idealization
learningObjectives: Explain why the clevis pin is modeled in double shear.
student: Is the pin at A in single shear or double shear? Explain using the clevis geometry.
instructor: The pin is in double shear because the inner member is located between two yoke arms. The load is transferred across two shear planes in the pin, one at each interface between the inner member and a clevis arm.
commonMistakes: If students use single shear, their pin shear stress will be twice the correct double-shear value.

title: Average Shear Stress in Pin A
learningObjectives: Compute average shear stress in a pin with multiple shear planes.
student: Determine the average shear stress in the pin at A.
instructor: τA = P/({{n_s}}AA) = {{clevis_load_N}} N / {{clevis_pin_total_shear_area_mm2}} mm2 = {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa. Equivalently, each shear plane carries V = {{clevis_shear_plane_load_N}} N, so τA = V/AA.

title: Largest Calculated Average Stress
learningObjectives: Compare average stress magnitudes across different checked components.
student: Among σ1, σ2, and τA, which calculated average stress has the largest magnitude?
instructor: The calculated average stresses are σ1 = {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa, σ2 = {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa, and τA = {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa. The largest average stress magnitude is {{clevis_largest_stress_mode}}, with magnitude {{clevis_largest_stress_MPa}} MPa.
gradingNotes: Emphasize that largest stress magnitude does not automatically mean governing failure unless allowable normal and shear strengths are known.

title: Optional Strength Factor of Safety Check
learningObjectives: Use allowable stresses to compute and interpret factors of safety.
student: Using the provided allowable normal stress and allowable pin shear stress, determine the factor of safety for each checked component and identify the governing checked mode.
instructor: FOS1 = σallow/σ1 = {{sigma_allow}} MPa / {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa = {{clevis_fos_1}}. FOS2 = σallow/σ2 = {{sigma_allow}} MPa / {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa = {{clevis_fos_2}}. FOSA = τallow/τA = {{tau_allow}} MPa / {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa = {{clevis_fos_pin}}. The smallest factor of safety is {{clevis_governing_fos}}, governed by {{clevis_governing_fos_mode}}.
gradingNotes: For the default allowables, the largest raw stress is in the right rod, but the smallest factor of safety is controlled by the relative allowable stresses. This is a useful distinction.

title: Connector Load and Additional Failure Modes
learningObjectives: Identify what the simplified connector analysis includes and excludes.
student: Identify the connector load carried by the pin and list additional connector failure modes that a detailed design would need to check.
instructor: The total load transferred by the pin is P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}. In the simplified model, this load is shared by {{n_s}} shear planes, so each plane carries {{clevis_shear_plane_load_N}} N. A detailed design could also require checks for bearing stress between the pin and holes, net-section tension of the yoke arms or inner member, tear-out, pin bending, contact pressure, wear, fatigue, and manufacturing tolerances.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited recommendation based on calculated stresses and missing design information.
student: Use the mechanics results to make a limited engineering recommendation. Identify the governing checked stress quantity and state what additional information would be needed to accept the connection for service.
instructor: For the simplified checks, σ1 = {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa, σ2 = {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa, and τA = {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa. The largest calculated average stress is {{clevis_largest_stress_mode}}. With the provided allowables, the governing factor of safety is {{clevis_governing_fos}} for {{clevis_governing_fos_mode}}. Before accepting the connection for service, an engineer should also verify material properties, appropriate design factor, bearing, net-section tension, tear-out, pin bending, fatigue if cyclic loading exists, clearances, and manufacturing tolerances.
gradingNotes: A good response does not overclaim safety from average stress alone. It states what has been checked and what still needs verification.
